content.title: About
content.content: Wild rice (Zizania aquatica) is the seed of an aquatic plant native to freshwater lakes and rivers of North America. Dry raw wild rice has a nutty flavor, light crunchy texture and is considered more nutritious than common white rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wild rice is not a true rice (it belongs to the grass family) but to the water‑grass family (Zizaniaceae).
It was a staple food for many Native American tribes and featured in ceremonial dishes.
The grains grow above water and are harvested by hand, often after they float to the surface.
Wild rice contains more protein and fiber than most other rice varieties.
In the United States, wild rice is the official state grain of Minnesota.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Wild rice provides about 14 % protein by weight, higher than most cereals.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for bone health and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: It raises blood sugar slowly, making it suitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Contains phenolic compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to wild rice.

items.title: Heavy‑metal content
items.content: Depending on the growing area, the grains can accumulate cadmium or lead; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: The high fiber content may cause gas or bloating in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse the dry wild rice and simmer for 45–60 minutes until tender. Use it in salads, soups, side dishes, vegetarian patties, or risotto. It also works well in breakfast porridges or rice pudding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store wild rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth.
